meta.description: Not Upton Sinclair. The line is David Starr Jordan's, printed in his 1922 memoir as Collis Huntington's 'code of power' — and used by Jordan from 1910.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Whatever is Not Nailed Down is Mine and Whatever I Can Pry Loose is Not Nailed Down'?
meta.ogDescription: Sinclair quoted it in 1923 and credited Dr. Jordan. The exact wording is David Starr Jordan's, from his 1922 memoir The Days of a Man.

answer.label: Not Upton Sinclair — actually David Starr Jordan
answer.authorDates: 1851–1931 · ichthyologist and founding president of Stanford University
answer.sourceLine: The familiar wording is Jordan’s own, printed in his memoir The Days of a Man, Volume One (World Book Company, 1922), page 479, where he gives it as the “code of power” by which the railroad baron Collis P. Huntington was “currently described.” Upton Sinclair did put a version of the saying in print in The Goose-Step (1923) — but he credited it to “Dr. Jordan” in the same sentence, and his wording is not the one that circulates.

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from

docMeta.dd: The Days of a Man, Volume One (1851–1899)
Two separate maxims in Jordan’s The Call of the Nation (American Unitarian Association, 1910), page 32

source.excerpt: Huntington, as is well known, maintained a rigid code of ethics of his own framing. It was, however, a code of power, currently described about as follows: “Whatever is not nailed down is mine. Whatever I can pry loose is not nailed down.”
trail: 1910 — Jordan prints the saying as two separate maxims in The Call of the Nation ↗, page 32: “Whatever is not nailed down is mine.” This is the motto of the exploiter. “Whatever can be pried loose is not nailed down.” No individual is named.

1922 — In his memoir The Days of a Man ↗, page 479, Jordan attaches the now-familiar single-speaker wording to Collis P. Huntington, calling it a “code of power” — a description of the man, not a quotation from him.
1923 — Upton Sinclair repeats the charge in The Goose-Step ↗, chapter XXXII, writing “Dr. Jordan described Huntington’s motto as…” and giving it in different words from the popular version.

1968 onward — writers begin putting the sentence in Huntington’s own mouth, in The Atlantic and then New York magazine; Quote Investigator ↗ tracks the drift and finds no evidence Huntington ever used it.
source.cutTag: The Days of a Man, Vol. 1, p. 479
source.excerptNote: Note Jordan’s hedge: the code is “currently described” this way. He never claims Huntington spoke the words — and Huntington had been dead since 1900.

author.name: David Starr Jordan
author.heading: Who was David Starr Jordan?
author.metaLine: 1851–1931 · Ichthyologist, founding president of Stanford University
author.bio: David Starr Jordan was an ichthyologist who served as the seventh president of Indiana University before becoming the founding president of Stanford University in 1891, staying in the post until 1913 and then serving as the university’s first chancellor until 1916. Outside the campus he was a conservationist and an outspoken antimilitarist, leading the World Peace Foundation from 1910 to 1914. He was also, less creditably, a committed supporter of eugenics — a strand of his public work that sits uneasily beside the reformist voice that produced this line.

copyAttribution: “Whatever is not nailed down is mine. Whatever I can pry loose is not nailed down.” — David Starr Jordan, The Days of a Man, Volume One (World Book Company, 1922), p. 479, describing Collis P. Huntington’s reputed “code of power.” Often miscredited to Upton Sinclair, who quoted it in 1923 while crediting Jordan, and to Huntington himself, for whom no evidence exists.

misattribution.heading: Two names get the credit. Neither claimed it.
misattribution.intro: This saying travels with a famous byline attached, and it has been attached to two different men — one who quoted it and named his source, and one who was dead before it appeared in print.

items.why: Sinclair really did print the saying, in The Goose-Step ↗ (1923), his study of American education. But the sentence he wrote is “Dr. Jordan described Huntington’s motto as: ‘Anything is mine that is not nailed down, and nothing is nailed that I can pry loose.’” The attribution is inside the quotation, and the wording is not the one that circulates today.

Quote sites hand the line to the railroad baron as a personal motto. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence he ever said it: Huntington died in 1900 ↗, and the earliest appearance QI documents is Jordan’s book of 1910.

items.who: Richard Ballinger and the Northwest fisheries
items.why: Jordan aimed the same line at President Taft’s Interior Secretary in a July 1910 New York Times interview and at Alaska and Washington fishing interests in 1915 and 1918, according to Quote Investigator ↗. They were the accused, never the speakers — the same move that later stuck the words to Huntington.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording that circulates today is Jordan’s own sentence about Huntington, printed in The Days of a Man ↗ in 1922 — an accusation by a critic, not a confession by a tycoon (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A conservationist’s accusation, not a tycoon’s boast
lead: Jordan wrote the line as conservation politics. In The Call of the Nation (1910) he argued that the United States had handed away its land, forests, coal and water power to anyone who asked, and set down “Whatever is not nailed down is mine” as “the motto of the exploiter,” following it with a second maxim — “Whatever can be pried loose is not nailed down” — that turns the first into a joke about how much can be levered away.

In his 1922 memoir he aimed both halves at one man: Collis P. Huntington, the Central Pacific baron whom Jordan, as Stanford’s president, blamed for endangering the fortune that funded the university. Jordan was careful in how he put it — Huntington’s code was “currently described” this way, he wrote, not spoken by Huntington — but that caution did not survive the retellings.
detailsBody: Jordan reused the saying for years against targets he disapproved of: Interior Secretary Richard Ballinger in a July 1910 New York Times interview, Alaska fisheries interests at a 1915 American Fisheries Society meeting, and again in 1918 on overfishing — each time as a philosophy he opposed, never as words anyone had actually spoken, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

By 1968 a reviewer in The Atlantic could describe it as “a remark … attributed to Huntington himself,” and a 1974 New York magazine article printed it as Huntington’s candor. Neither traced it back to Jordan, and the chain of paraphrase quietly moved the sentence from the accuser to the accused (Quote Investigator ↗).
context.pull: A critic’s caricature, reprinted often enough, became the villain’s own boast.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator found no substantive evidence Collis Huntington said the line; David Starr Jordan popularized it starting in 1910 as the “motto of the exploiter”; Jordan linked it to Huntington’s “code of ethics” in 1922; Upton Sinclair echoed Jordan in 1923; by the 1960s–70s (Atlantic 1968, New York 1974) writers ascribed it to Huntington himself.

Jordan’s The Days of a Man, Volume One (1851–1899), World Book Company, Yonkers-on-Hudson, 1922, page 479, contains: “Huntington, as is well known, maintained a rigid code of ethics of his own framing. It was, however, a code of power, currently described about as follows: ‘Whatever is not nailed down is mine. Whatever I can pry loose is not nailed down.’” Verified in the scanned full text (page marker 478 precedes the passage; 479 is its page).

Jordan’s The Call of the Nation (American Unitarian Association, Boston, 1910), page 32, contains: “Whatever is not nailed down is mine.” This is the motto of the exploiter. “Whatever can be pried loose is not nailed down.” This is the second maxim… Verified in the scanned full text.

Upton Sinclair’s The Goose-Step (1923), chapter XXXII “The Story of Stanford” (running head page 153), contains: “Dr. Jordan described Huntington’s motto as: ‘Anything is mine that is not nailed down, and nothing is nailed that I can pry loose.’” Verified in the scanned full text.

David Starr Jordan lived 1851–1931, was an ichthyologist, seventh president of Indiana University (1885–1891), founding president of Stanford University (1891–1913) and its first chancellor (1913–1916), led the World Peace Foundation 1910–1914, and was a supporter of eugenics.
Collis P. Huntington lived 22 October 1821 to 13 August 1900 and was one of the Big Four who formed the Central Pacific Railroad in 1861, reputed the most ruthless of the four.
